newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin and Russian PM plot government reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin and Russian PM plot government reshuffle.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin met his prime minister on Tuesday to put the finishing touches to a government shake-up and scolded Russia's chief prosecutor in a new effort to reassert his authority after illness.

Yeltsin, back in the Kremlin after eight months fighting heart problems and then pneumonia, met Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to discuss a reshuffle which is expected to be announced after he addresses parliament on Thursday.
Presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky gave no clues about what changes they planned but said they may not be as far-reaching as has been predicted.
Chernomyrdin promised last week the reshuffle would be more than cosmetic, but Yastrzhembsky told Interfax news agency on Tuesday it would not be "as global as some mass media write".
Some media have said Chernomyrdin may fall in the reshuffle, demanded by Yeltsin over the government's failure to pay wages on time, but his departure looks increasingly unlikely.
Attention has switched largely to the ministers dealing with the economy and social policy and to Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, who was given a dressing down by Yeltsin last week.

Speculation has also centred on whether Anatoly Chubais, the influential chief of the Kremlin staff and an instigator of market reforms in Russia, will be given a formal role in the government to oversee the economy.
A government spokesman said Chernomyrdin was working on recommendations for the reshuffle but also indicated there may be no radical changes in the line-up.

"The prime minister thinks that various socio-political figures and the mass media are paying a disproportionate amount of attention to the matter of the proposed changes in the government," spokesman Igor Shabdurasulov said.
"The most fanciful personnel changes are raised when it is a question above all of serious structural reorganisation."
Yeltsin, 66, looked in good form in brief television footage of him greeting Chernomyrdin, who is a loyal ally but has been under fire over the failure to pay wages in the state sector.

The president chided Chernomyrdin last week but his main aim may have been to create the impression that he is firmly in charge and means to tackle the economic and political problems that have piled up during his absence from the Kremlin.

The Kremlin did not immediately release details of Yeltsin's meeting with Chernomyrdin, although Yastrzhembsky said they would also discuss plans for Yeltsin's summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton in Helsinki on March 21-21.

Yeltsin also had talks with Prosecutor-General Yuri Skuratov. Russian television showed Yeltsin criticising Skuratov, who stared in silence at the president as he sat across the table from him in the Kremlin.
Yeltsin said he was dissatisfied with his work and warned him that public anger was rising over his failure to solve a growing list of high-profile murders.
"Behind the overall figures, which I am well acquainted with, are hidden some prominent murders which the whole of society is seething about," Interfax quoted Yeltsin as saying.

Crime, much of it involving mafia-style gangs, has risen sharply since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991. Skuratov has been ridiculed by the media for failing to solve any of the prominent murder cases.
Crime is expected to be one of the main themes in Yeltsin's annual address to parliament on Thursday in which he will set out his polices for the year ahead.
The speech, expected to last 40 minutes, will be his longest public appearance since he fell ill before his re-election last July and is seen as a test of his recovery and ability to rule.
